title: Debug logging left enabled fills the log disk and breaks request handling
source_note: Failure pattern (a temporary diagnostic setting - here verbose logging - left enabled after an earlier investigation, filling a disk until the service cannot write) is a common operational class in the Google SRE Book's troubleshooting chapter. All services, log lines, metrics, and timestamps are fabricated for evaluation.
incident_report: Since ~14:03 UTC api-server is throwing 5xx on a growing share of requests. It looks host-specific - some hosts are fine. No deploys. There was a troubleshooting session on this service about an hour ago.

signal_lines.msg: log level set to DEBUG on host pool (troubleshooting session)
disk full: cannot write request log; /var/log at 100%
request handling failing: cannot create temp file (No space left on device)
5xx rate 22%; errors correlate with hosts at 100% disk
log level reverted to INFO; old debug logs rotated; disk at 61%

ground_truth.root_cause: DEBUG-level logging was enabled on the api-server host pool during an earlier troubleshooting session (~1 hour before) and never reverted. The elevated log volume filled the /var/log disk to 100%. With the disk full, api-server could not write its request log or create temp files ('No space left on device'), so a growing fraction of requests failed - tracking exactly the hosts that hit 100% disk. Recovery required reverting the log level and rotating the accumulated debug logs.
evidence_path: api-server INFO ~1h before: log level set to DEBUG on the host pool for a troubleshooting session
api-server ERROR: disk full, cannot write request log / create temp files (No space left on device)
error_rate rises to ~22%, correlated with the hosts at 100% disk
recovery after the log level is reverted to INFO and old debug logs are rotated
ground_truth.fix: Revert the log level and rotate the debug logs (done). Make elevated log levels time-boxed with automatic revert, alert on disk usage well before 100%, and keep application temp files off the log volume.
